title: Where the Water Goes
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 5 of 10
content:
Maui's fishhook could move stone, calm a snarled rope, and turn its owner into an alarming number of animals. It could not persuade a tiny brass compass to point north.

“Defective,” he announced.

“You keep holding it beside the hook.”

“Which should make it grateful.”

The compass was Neri's. It had begun spinning three days earlier, when a Threadway opened at the foot of Tideglass Cove and let in a cold tide from somewhere none of us recognized. The current was taking sand from the beach and pulling it toward a crack beneath the rocks.

If it continued, the little harbor would lose its shelter.

Maui wanted to plug the crack with a boulder. I wanted to map the current first.

We argued on the shore while seabirds wheeled overhead.

“You're making a plan for a puddle,” he said.

“It's an inlet with moving water.”

“Very threatening water.”

“It might be, if you stop pretending the only answer is being bigger than the problem.”

His face closed.

I regretted the sharpness before I had finished speaking, but I did not apologize for the idea.

“I'm going to measure it,” I said. “You can help, or not.”

I took string, weights, and strips of colored cloth down the beach. After a long silence, Maui picked up the heaviest bundle.

“Tell me where,” he said.

For two hours we tracked the current. The water was not trying to drag the shore away. It was being pulled through a doorway beneath the rocks, one that had opened unevenly and become stuck.

Maui knelt beside the opening.

“So. Boulder's a bad idea.”

“Spectacularly.”

He gave me a narrow look. “Enjoy this moment. It is rare.”

We could not decide what to call the doorway.

Neri said *tide arch*, because the old survey marked the waterline beside it. Maui said *the world's worst bathtub plug*, which was not a name I intended to write in the records. I called it *the lower Tideglass Threadway* on my first page and then underlined *provisional* beside the name.

Fen, the tidekeeper, met us on the sand with a weighted cord and a sour expression.

"You're both standing where the bank slipped yesterday," they said.

Maui looked at the sand beneath his feet. "This bank?"

"Yes."

He moved. I followed him, somewhat less proudly.

Fen showed us yesterday's marks: a dark line left by high tide, a fan of pebbles where the current had turned, and a narrow groove cut through the sediment. Whatever the unstable opening was doing, it wasn't merely making a compass misbehave. It was redirecting the water that sheltered fishing boats.

"If we block it," Fen said, "the pressure will look for another weakness. If we leave it, the sand will move out of the harbor."

Maui frowned. "So both choices are bad."

"Unmeasured choices are bad," Fen replied. "Let's find one we can understand."

I liked Fen immediately.

We tied strips of blue and red cloth to separate lengths of line and set them in the current from a safe point on the rock. The red strip swung toward the inlet and stayed there; the blue one tugged outward, catching a counterflow against the submerged stone. I recorded their movements while Fen called tide intervals. Maui held the weighted rope steady with a care I hadn't expected.

My pencil broke.

"Of course," I muttered.

Maui handed me a charcoal stub from his pouch.

"You carry charcoal?" I asked.

"For writing my own magnificent praises."

"Naturally."

"Also for fire-starting."

"Less magnificent."

"Not when you're cold."

I drew a second diagram on the back of Neri's discarded receipt. The pattern made sense: the bent ring was keeping one side of the arch open. Water entered at the wrong moment, not as an ordinary tide but as a narrow, powerful crosscurrent. The harbor did not need a heroic boulder. It needed that hinge seated correctly, and it needed a way to check that the fix held after the tide changed.

Fen studied the sketch.

"Can you reach the ring without standing in the pull?"

"Only if Maui lifts the outer slab," I said. "And only if you keep the line attached to both of us."

Maui opened his mouth to object to needing a rope.

Fen raised an eyebrow.

He closed it.

"Fine," he said. "A very heroic rope."

The first attempt failed. The slab shifted, grit slid across the ring, and I had to pull my hand back before the metal caught my sleeve. Maui held the weight while Fen called a halt.

"Again?" Maui asked.

"Not until we check the tether," Fen replied.

I was shaking. It took me an embarrassing moment to admit it.

"Could we stop for five minutes?" I asked.

Maui looked at me. "Of course."

During the break, Fen unrolled a second chart across the rock. It showed where the current ran at low tide and how far it shifted when the cold Threadway water pushed through.

"There's a difference between a temporary surge and a changed channel," they said. "If we force that ring now, we might get through the first one and still leave the harbor worse next week."

I traced the lines with a finger. The hand that had drawn the little lantern bracket the day before wanted to leap ahead to a solution. My legs were trembling from the first attempt.

"Can we compare it with yesterday's waterline?" I asked.

Fen pointed to a chalk mark under the rock ledge. "That's why we measured it."

Maui crouched beside us. He looked at the chalk, then at the boulder he'd suggested using as a plug.

"So if I block the opening, the water finds somewhere else."

"Possibly through somebody's landing," Fen said.

He sighed. "My boulder has become unpopular."

I wanted to tease him. Instead I passed him the rope and asked if he'd help mark the next safe position.

He tied one knot, then stopped. "This kind?"

"Show Fen."

Fen checked it and made him redo the loose turn. He didn't argue. When the rope finally held the strain under a controlled pull, he looked delighted in a quieter way than I'd ever seen.

"Is this what ordinary sailors do?" he asked.

"Among other things," Fen said.

"Exhausting."

I laughed, and the tension in my shoulders eased. We still had a dangerous mechanism to inspect. Nobody had made it safe just by being brave. But we had a measured window, a better tether, and permission to stop when the conditions changed.

When we tried again, I counted aloud rather than letting everyone imagine they knew what I was thinking. Maui waited for the count. That, more than his strength, made me trust the attempt.

I sat on the high dry rock and drank water. My hands had remembered the shape of the mechanism, but they still belonged to a person who could be frightened. Nobody called me weak. Fen marked the next safe window, and Maui sat beside me without turning my pause into a lecture.

"Still think the boulder would work?" I asked.

"Absolutely," he said. "For making a larger disaster."

I laughed, then felt brave enough to stand again.

On the second attempt, we reset the ring a fraction at a time. I asked Maui to shift the stone; he waited for my instruction. Fen watched the tide marks and gave us room to stop whenever the water changed. When the blue cloth released from the pull, all three of us saw it.

"Hold," Fen called.

We held.

The ring settled. The line slackened.

We didn't celebrate until Fen finished the last measurement.

We worked together. He shifted the rocks enough for me to reach the bent brass ring at the heart of the door. I adjusted it, checked where the pressure would go, and used the blue thread from my old key to mark the safe alignment. When Maui returned the last stone, the inlet took a breath and settled.

The compass stopped spinning.

At sunset, we sat above the cove with sand in our shoes. I nudged his shoulder.

“You didn't have to let me win the argument.”

“I didn't.”

I looked at him.

“You were right,” he said. “That's different.”

The admission cost him something. I could see it in the way his hand tightened around the hook.

“Does being wrong hurt?” I asked.

He laughed without humor. “When everyone expects you to save them? Yes.”

I thought of the voice from my memory, the one that had taught me usefulness was a debt.

“I know that feeling,” I said.

For a while we watched the water go where it was meant to go.

Then Maui asked whether I wanted him to teach me to steer by stars that changed their positions every night. I asked whether he could actually do that.

“No,” he said. “But it sounds like a magnificent challenge.”

I took his offered hand to stand.

For once the horizon didn't seem to be demanding that either of us prove we deserved to be standing in front of it.
